Upcoming Pause in Configuration Changes

Aug 10, 2026

As previously communicated, the Office of MaineCare Services is launching an upgraded MIHMS, our claims processing system, in October 2026. To support system readiness activities, MaineCare is temporarily pausing the implementation of configuration changes from the end of August to the end of October.

Coding and NDC Requests

Continue submitting coding requests to OMS.referencefile@maine.gov and NDC/J-Code Requests to MaineCareNDCrequest.DHHS@maine.gov. Requests submitted by August 19, 2026, if approved, will be implemented no later than the last synchronization on August 25, 2026. Continue to submit these requests as usual after these dates. MaineCare will review and document change requests beginning at the end of October.

Rate Change Requests

Continue submitting rate change requests as usual to MIHMSRateRqst.DHHS@maine.gov throughout this period. MaineCare will review and document change requests as appropriate for implementation beginning at the end of October.

Claims and Billing Inquiries

Continue directing claims and billing inquiries to Provider Services at 1-866-690-5585. We will continue reviewing claim denials to determine if a configuration change is needed. MaineCare will review and document change requests as appropriate for implementation before the configuration pause or beginning at the end of October.

We appreciate your continued cooperation during this transition. If you have questions about the configuration pause or the status of a request, please contact your Provider Relations Specialist.

Hello, this is Governor Janet Mills, and thank you for listening.

Well, you know, one of the lessons learned from the pandemic time was how dependent we are as a state and community on producers from other states and other countries for basic goods like food, textiles, and construction materials. It occurred to me that our growing season is too incredibly short for us to become as self-reliant as we should be.

And after the pandemic disrupted markets and caused food shortages nationwide, we realized it was very important to have locally grown, fresh food right here in Maine and help our local farmers. So I used federal funding through my Jobs and Recovery Plan to provide grants to farmers to buy equipment to meet that higher demand for locally grown food, and I began to look for other ways to extend our growing season here in Maine.

Well, one of the things you can do is to provide greenhouses to communities who are able to support them and help people of all ages learn how to grow their own food. I called on the Legislature to provide one-time funds through the state biennial budget to buy greenhouses for as many schools and communities as possible. That will strengthen our supply of local food and will teach kids and families to grow their own food and extend the growing season.

The Legislature funded that proposal, and I'm proud to announce that we're now awarding grants to communities across Maine to expand their local food production and education programs through durable shared-use greenhouses. These grants were awarded through a competitive process. The organizations applied for them, and they include the Alfond Youth and Community Center in Waterville, where they're going to install a greenhouse to expand local food production and youth education. 

The Healthy Island Project in Stonington will use a greenhouse to increase access to fresh, locally grown food. And the Portland Community Squash will install a greenhouse to send more fresh produce home to low-income families and teach Portland Public School students how to grow their own food. Limestone Community School will install a greenhouse to expand their outdoor science program and provide students with hands on learning in nutrition, agriculture, and environmental science. And they'll run a student-run farmers market—I think that's great.

Over the past eight years, my Administration has invested more than $60 million in Maine farms and local agriculture, supporting the purchase of locally grown food, helping farmers expand their operations and equipment, strengthening our food system, and keeping Maine's farming heritage thriving.

You know, my grandparents were potato farmers in Ashland. I hope they would be proud that their granddaughter insisted that the state budget include a small amount of money for community greenhouses across the state. Sort of like the Victory Gardens of World War II and decades past, places where people of all ages can learn something about nutrition and how to grow lettuce, peppers, and parsley; where the older folks can teach the younger folks about the value of homegrown tomatoes and cucumbers and such and talk with each other in community. Where they can feel the joy of growing their own healthy food and appreciate what their neighbors are doing and appreciate their own Maine roots, the way I appreciate mine.

Dave Mallett, one of my good friends, the singer who passed away last year, used to sing a very popular song: "Inch by inch, row by row. Gonna make this garden grow. All it takes is a rake and a hoe and a piece of fertile ground."

Well, we're going to have everybody singing those songs in Maine in honor of Dave Mallett, and in honor of our agricultural heritage and the state of Maine's ability to become independent and self-reliant by community greenhouses.

This is Governor Janet Mills, and thank you for listening.

Breaking: Active Cyber Breaches Affecting Public Water Systems Demand Immediate Action.

The US EPA, FBI, Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), and Water Information Sharing & Analysis Center (WaterISAC) have held urgent briefings regarding active and on-going cybersecurity breaches at dozens of Public Water Systems (PWSs) in at least seven states across the U.S. The targeted PWSs range in size from small to large.

Many wastewater systems use similar technology as found in the drinking water sector. A common symptom of these breaches includes a loss of PLC connectivity with devices. These incidents all involve vulnerabilities related to PLCs, as described in the Iranian-Affiliated Cyber Actors Exploit Programmable Logic Controllers Across US Critical Infrastructure advisory (PDF).

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has information and guidance regarding malicious cyber actors targeting PLCs.

Aug 06, 2026

The American Medical Association (AMA) announced maternity care services code changes that will be effective January 1, 2027. These changes include the removal of 17 billing codes, the addition of 12 billing codes, and revisions to 6 billing codes to reflect modern obstetric practices, allow for more accurate and transparent reporting, and to create a data foundation to better attribute maternal care and support the complexities of team-based care throughout a patient's journey.

In preparation for these changes, MaineCare is also making changes to coding requirements for maternity care services, including the transition to non-global and non-bundled care coding and reimbursement. To ensure consistent reimbursement MaineCare is directing providers to take the following actions no later than prior to September 1, 2026:

  • Adjust maternity care visit billing from global or bundled service codes to Evaluation and Management (E/M) service codes based on each member’s estimated due date and the anticipated number of visits for the remainder of their antepartum period in accordance with AMA Antepartum Transition Reporting guidance;.
  • Append the TH modifier for all maternity care E/M service codes on your claim to identify the visit as a maternity care service;
  • Transition from total-visit tracking to individual encounter documentation, as each prenatal and postpartum visit must now independently support standard E/M complexity or time rules; and
  • Monitor professional guidance from organizations like the American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology and the AMA to prepare billers and systems for the significant coding changes to be effective on January 1, 2027.

Competitive Skills Scholarship Program (CSSP) Rule Changes Effective August 2, 2026

August 5, 2026

The Maine Department of Labor has updated the Competitive Skills Scholarship Program (CSSP) rules to implement recent statutory changes, expand participant supports, improve program flexibility, and clarify program requirements. The revised rules took effect on August 2, 2026.

Some of the most significant changes include:

  • Expanded monthly stipend eligibility. More students may now qualify for a monthly CSSP stipend because income eligibility limits have increased.
  • Partial stipends for part-time students. Eligible part-time students may now receive a prorated monthly stipend based on their enrollment status and income.
  • Expanded support services. Eligible participants may qualify for increased assistance with transportation, vehicle repairs, and other necessary needs under higher support service funding limits.
  • Expanded educational opportunities. Eligibility has also been expanded for applicants with pre-existing preparatory associate degree programs.
  • Improved program clarity and accessibility. The revised rules simplify eligibility requirements, clarify appeal rights, improve communication preferences, and increase transparency regarding the High-Wage, In-Demand Occupations list.
  • New CSSP Cohort funding opportunities. Training providers and their partners will be invited to apply for CSSP Cohort funding. The Maine Department of Labor will host a listening session to gather feedback on implementation before issuing a Request for Applications (RFA) for pilot cohort programs.

For those interested in reviewing the complete rule changes, including the final adopted rule, tracked changes, and the Department's Summary of Comments and Responses from the rulemaking process, please visit the Maine Department of Labor Rulemaking webpage: https://www.maine.gov/labor/rulemaking/

CSSP Cohort Listening Session

Community members interested in learning more about the CSSP Cohort model are invited to join a listening session on September 18th, at 10:00 a.m. to share ideas, discuss opportunities to expand access, and help identify implementation priorities.

Zoom Registration: https://mainestate.zoom.us/meeting/register/-vPlt9ZbSG23mGKG96bmsg

Current CSSP participants will receive a separate email describing the rule changes and inviting them to schedule a meeting with their CSSP case manager to review whether they may qualify for additional benefits under the new rules.

Thank you for your continued partnership in helping Maine people access education, training, and employment through the Competitive Skills Scholarship Program.

Public Guidance Statement RE: HUD's New Emotional Support Animal Enforcement Guidance and 
Maine Housing Providers' Continuing Obligations Under the Maine Human Rights Act 
August 4, 2026 
What Has Changed at the Federal Level 
On May 22, 2026, the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) issued an enforcement 
memorandum announcing that it will no longer find reasonable cause in housing complaints involving 
emotional support animals (ESAs). In other words, animals that provide comfort, companionship, or otherwise 
mitigate the effects of a person’s disability but have not been individually trained to perform specific 
disability-related tasks are no longer protected at the federal level. Going forward, HUD will pursue 
enforcement only where an animal has been trained to perform work or tasks directly related to a person's 
disability (essentially, HUD has imported the Americans with Disabilities Act's narrower "service animal" 
definition into Fair Housing Act enforcement).

individuals who rely on ESAs as part of their disability-related care. After 35 years without updating its 
regulations in this area, the federal government's chosen solution has been, perhaps unsurprisingly, to reduce 
protections rather than clarify them. 
The Maine Human Rights Commission takes note of this development. We also take note that it changes

items.title: US Department of Labor finds child labor and wage violations  at 3 San Antonio bakery and café locations — U.S. Department of Labor — News Releases
items.content_text: SAN ANTONIO – The U.S. Department of Labor has recovered thousands in back wages and assessed penalties after a federal investigation revealed child labor, minimum wage, and overtime violations by the operators of three La Panaderia Bakery & Café locations in San Antonio.The department’s Wage and Hour Division investigated the pay practices of Tequila Almond Croissant LLC, Pan Dulce LLC, and SA Bakery Co. LLC. All three do business as La Panaderia Bakery & Café in San Antonio with locations at 301 E. Houston Street; 17030 Fiesta Texas Drive; and 8305 Broadway.Division investigators found the employers violated child labor provisions of the Fair Labor Standards Act. Specifically, they employed a 13-year-old minor who was under the legal age for employment and permitted a 15-year-old minor to work overnight, which is prohibited for 14- and 15-year-olds. The division assessed a $25,706 civil money penalty for the child labor violations.The division’s investigation also revealed minimum wage violations due to the employers’ failure to pay one worker for two overnight shifts at the La Cantera café location on Fiesta Texas Drive. The employers also failed to combine hours for employees who worked at multiple café locations and paid the employees straight-time rates instead of the required time-and-one-half overtime rates. Employers and workers can contact the division with questions and requests for compliance assistance at its toll-free helpline, 866-4US-WAGE (487-9243). Employers are also encouraged to use the agency’s industry-specific compliance assistance toolkits to learn about their responsibilities under the laws enforced by the division. The agency’s PAID program offers employers an opportunity to self-report and resolve potential minimum wage and overtime violations under the FLSA, as well as certain potential violations under the Family and Medical Leave Act.Download the agency’s free timesheet app for iOS and Android devices to track hours and pay.

The employers also failed to combine hours for employees who worked at multiple café locations and paid the employees straight-time rates instead of the required time-and-one-half overtime rates. Employers and workers can contact the division with questions and requests for compliance assistance at its toll-free helpline, 866-4US-WAGE (487-9243). Employers are also encouraged to use the agency’s industry-specific compliance assistance toolkits to learn about their responsibilities under the laws enforced by the division. The agency’s PAID program offers employers an opportunity to self-report and resolve potential minimum wage and overtime violations under the FLSA, as well as certain potential violations under the Family and Medical Leave Act.Download the agency’s free timesheet app for iOS and Android devices to track hours and pay.

AUGUSTA, MAINE
– The Secretary of State’s Office today announced that Maine voters may now request absentee ballots for the November 3, 2026 General Election. Voters may
request ballots online
or by contacting their town or city clerk. Contact
information for municipal clerks
can be found on the Secretary of State website.
Maine’s no-excuse absentee voting laws allows any registered voter to request a ballot three months before Election Day, and their ballots will be issued by their municipal clerks beginning 30 days prior to Election Day. Once a ballot request is submitted, Maine voters can
track the process of that request and their ballot
online.
Maine’s no-excuse absentee voting period, including in-person absentee voting at town and city halls, extends through October 29. All absentee ballots for the upcoming General Election must be received by a voter’s municipality by 8 p.m. on November 3, 2026.

items.content_text: The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), Office of Pharmacy Affairs (OPA), which administers the 340B Drug Pricing Program (340B Program), is issuing this Notice to announce the availability of a revised 340B Rebate Model Pilot Program (Pilot). The Pilot provides a rebate mechanism through which qualifying drug manufacturers may effectuate the 340B ceiling price for certain drugs sold to covered entities. Consistent with HRSA's longstanding statutory authority, rebates will be used instead of upfront discounts. HRSA issued a Request for Information (RFI) \1\ to gather input from interested parties regarding the potential use of rebates to effectuate the ceiling price under the 340B Program, including the standards and procedures that should govern the approval of manufacturer rebate plans and the impacts on all stakeholders. After carefully considering all comments from interested parties and different policy alternatives, HRSA is announcing this Pilot, which will implement a rebate approach for a limited set of drugs, and which builds on established and successful rebate programs. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Provider Responsibility Regarding Third Party Liability and Secondary Billing

Aug 03, 2026

In a previous notice, the Office of MaineCare Services (OMS) reminded providers of your responsibilities regarding third -party liability and secondary billing. Pursuant to MaineCare Benefits Manual (MBM) Ch. I Section 1.07-3(B), MaineCare is the payor of last resort. OMS announced that we will update the billing and claims system requirements to accurately reflect the provider’s obligation to bill primary insurance when other coverage is available.

Effective August 10, 2026, our claims system will no longer treat most Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) and Healthcare Common Procedure Coding System (HCPCS) codes as exempt from billing the primary commercial carrier. In accordance with MBM Ch. I Section 1.07: Third Party Liability, providers must seek payment from the primary carrier before billing MaineCare for all claims for these services for members with primary coverage, even when:

  • the billing codes for same services vary between payors; and
  • the primary payor’s service coverage applies only to a portion of the MaineCare defined service. For example, this applies when the MaineCare service is more comprehensive than the primary payor’s coverage.

MaineCare also recognizes that many provider types that were previously unable to enroll in Medicare can now enroll and bill Medicare as the primary payor for services delivered to members dually eligible for Medicare and Medicaid. Providers eligible to enroll with Medicare to deliver Medicare reimbursable services must do so to receive MaineCare reimbursement as a secondary payor.

MaineCare’s claims system will accept an Explanation of Benefits (EOB) with primary dollars attached even if the billing codes differ. The system will process secondary claims as long as the provider, member, dates of service, and billed charges match. Providers must use the most specific code possible to maintain billing integrity and to comply with correct claim submission procedures.

Please monitor MaineCare e-messages for future communications on this topic as continued reviews and necessary system changes occur. We appreciate your efforts to preserve MaineCare funding and ensure compliance with these requirements.

For questions, please contact your Provider Relations Specialist.

Baldacci. Third-party defendants Steven Foss, Maggie Morse -Foss and Mofo, LLC (the “Foss

concludes that (1) it does not have jurisdiction over plaintiff’s complaint and (2) the third -party 
complaint should be stayed.
